chapters.title: Chapter 3: Case Studies in Currency Wars

lessons.title: Japan's Yen Interventions and the Carry Trade

body.text: Japan's currency story runs backwards from the usual currency war script. In 1985 the world deliberately made the yen stronger. Four decades later, a single 25 basis point rate hike in Tokyo was enough to trigger one of the sharpest global market shocks in years, purely because of how much of the world had spent two decades borrowing in yen.

children.text: 1985: When the World Deliberately Weakened the Dollar, Not the Yen

markDefs.definition: The 1985 agreement between the US, Japan, West Germany, France and the UK to coordinate intervention that would depreciate the US dollar against the yen and Deutsche mark, addressing an unsustainable US trade deficit.

children.text: On 22 September 1985, finance ministers from the US, Japan, West Germany, France and the UK met at New York's Plaza Hotel and agreed to coordinate intervention to push the dollar down against the yen and Deutsche mark, addressing a US trade deficit that had become politically unbearable. The
worked with startling force: the yen strengthened from around 240 to the dollar in 1985 to around 120 by 1988, roughly doubling in value in under three years.

markDefs.definition: A Japanese term for the recession caused by a rapidly appreciating yen, first used to describe the export-sector slowdown that followed the Plaza Accord's currency shift.

children.text: This is the opposite of every devaluation covered so far in this course: a coordinated, deliberate strengthening of a currency, agreed jointly by five governments. But a yen that strong, that fast, hurt Japan's exporters badly enough to produce what the Japanese press called

, the yen-appreciation recession. Japan's response, aggressive monetary easing to soften the export hit, is widely blamed as a major contributor to the asset bubble that inflated through the late 1980s and then collapsed into the deflationary 'lost decades' that followed.
Decades of Near-Zero Rates Made the Yen the World's Funding Currency

Fighting deflation through the 1990s and 2000s, the Bank of Japan cut rates to zero in 1999 and eventually to negative territory in 2016, holding them there for the better part of two decades. Whatever this did for Japan's own economy, it had a huge side effect on global markets: with borrowing costs in yen near zero for so long, the yen became the world's default funding currency for the carry trade covered earlier in this course, borrow cheap yen, invest the proceeds in higher-yielding assets almost anywhere else in the world.

body.text: Notice what this quietly built up over twenty-plus years: an enormous, hard-to-measure stock of global positions funded in yen, from developed-market bonds to emerging-market equities. As long as Japanese rates stayed near zero and the yen stayed weak, this trade was comfortable. The risk was never really about Japan's economy. It was about what happens to every other market in the world if that funding source suddenly gets more expensive.

children.text: August 2024: When the Carry Trade Unwound

On 31 July 2024, the Bank of Japan raised its policy rate to around 0.25%, a genuinely small move in absolute terms, its second hike since ending negative rates earlier that year. Days later, a weaker-than-expected US jobs report raised fears of a US slowdown, narrowing the US-Japan rate gap from both directions at once. For a trade built on that gap staying wide and stable for years, this was enough to trigger a rapid, disorderly unwind.

events.title: BOJ raises rates to ~0.25%
events.description: A small hike in absolute terms, but a meaningful signal after decades of near-zero or negative Japanese rates.

events.title: Weak US jobs report
events.description: Disappointing US employment data fuels fears of a sharper-than-expected US slowdown, pressuring the dollar and narrowing the US-Japan rate gap further.

events.title: Global markets sell off sharply
events.description: The yen strengthens rapidly as leveraged carry positions unwind; Japan's Nikkei 225 falls by roughly 12%, its worst single-day percentage drop since October 1987, and equity markets globally, including India's Nifty and Sensex, fall sharply the same week.
Markets stabilise as the BOJ signals a cautious approach to further hikes and volatility subsides, though the episode leaves carry trade positioning permanently more cautious.

body.title: Size the Yen's Move
body.prompt: The yen strengthened from approximately ¥161 to the dollar in mid-July 2024 to approximately ¥141 to the dollar within about a week during the August 2024 unwind. Approximately what percentage did the yen appreciate against the dollar over this move? Round to the nearest whole percent.
body.explanation: (161 − 141) / 161 ≈ 12.4%. A double-digit percentage currency move within about a week, in either direction, is extreme by major-currency standards, and is exactly the kind of move that forces leveraged carry positions to close all at once rather than gradually.

body.text: A quarter-point rate hike is a routine central bank decision almost anywhere else in the world. The reason this one moved global equity markets, not just currency markets, is scale: after two decades of near-zero Japanese rates, the yen-funded carry trade had grown large enough that even a small change at the margin forced a disorderly scramble to buy back yen and sell the risk assets it had funded. This is the leverage lesson underneath every carry trade discussed in this course: the position that looks safest during calm markets is often the one that moves fastest and furthest once the funding cost changes.

body.caption: Two Very Different Ways Japan Has Moved the Yen

cells: Coordinated multilateral intervention by five governments
Yen weakens after a disaster-driven spike
A modest BOJ rate hike triggers leveraged position unwinding globally
The BOJ's hike was deliberate; the scale of the market reaction was not

body.title: Quick Check: What Actually Caused the August 2024 Selloff?
body.question: The BOJ's July 2024 rate hike, to roughly 0.25%, was small by the standards of most central banks. Why did it still trigger a sharp global equity selloff?
options: Because the Bank of Japan announced it was deliberately trying to crash global stock markets
Because decades of near-zero Japanese rates had built up a large stock of yen-funded carry trades, and even a small narrowing of the rate gap was enough to force a disorderly, leveraged unwind
Because the yen is pegged to the dollar and any rate change automatically triggers a fixed devaluation
Because Japan's stock market has no connection to global equity markets
body.explanation: The size of the shock came from position scale built up over years, not from the size of the rate move itself. This is a recurring pattern worth remembering: it's not always the biggest policy change that causes the biggest market reaction, it's the policy change that hits the most crowded, leveraged positioning.

body.title: You Manage a Multi-Asset Fund With Yen-Funded Positions
body.scenario: Your fund has been running a modest yen-funded carry position for two years, borrowing yen at near-zero cost to hold higher-yielding emerging market bonds, including some Indian debt. It is late July 2024, and the BOJ has just hiked rates for the second time this year, with commentary suggesting it is not finished normalising policy.
body.prompt: Do you unwind the position pre-emptively, hold it, or reduce it partially? Justify your choice given what this lesson has covered.
body.modelAnswer: Reduce it partially rather than holding the full position or exiting entirely. The lesson here is that positioning scale, not the size of any single rate move, is what turns an orderly policy normalisation into a disorderly market event. With the BOJ signalling it isn't finished, the rate gap this trade depends on is structurally narrowing, not just moving once, which raises the odds of a further, possibly sharper, unwind later. Holding the full position bets that you can react faster than the rest of the market when the next move comes, a bet that August 2024 showed can fail badly given how fast these moves happen. Exiting entirely gives up carry income for a normalisation that may still take years to fully play out. Trimming the position now locks in some of the gains, reduces exposure to a sudden violent unwind, and keeps some carry income if the BOJ moves slowly, the more balanced response to a trade whose core risk is timing a crowded exit rather than the underlying rate differential itself.

cards.definition: A coordinated agreement among five governments to depreciate the US dollar against the yen and Deutsche mark, which roughly doubled the yen's value against the dollar by 1988.
Japanese term for a recession caused by rapid yen appreciation, first used after the Plaza Accord's effects on Japanese exporters.
Borrowing yen at near-zero or negative rates to invest in higher-yielding assets elsewhere, a trade that grew enormous over two decades of ultra-low Japanese rates.
A rapid, often disorderly reversal of carry trade positions, typically triggered by a narrowing rate differential or rising volatility, as seen in August 2024.

points: The 1985 Plaza Accord shows currency intervention can run in the opposite direction from every other episode in this course: a deliberate, coordinated strengthening rather than a devaluation.
Two decades of near-zero and negative Japanese interest rates made the yen the world's default carry trade funding currency, building up a large, hard-to-measure stock of leveraged global positions.
The August 2024 unwind shows that a small, routine-looking rate hike can trigger an outsized global market reaction when it hits crowded, leveraged positioning built up over years.

The yen strengthened by roughly 12% against the dollar within about a week in August 2024, and Japan's Nikkei fell by its sharpest single-day percentage since 1987, with Indian and other global markets also selling off sharply the same week.
Not every large currency move is a deliberate policy choice. Some, like the 2024 unwind, are the market's own reaction to a much smaller policy change meeting an unusually large, fragile position.
The next lesson turns fully to how Indian markets specifically respond when episodes like these hit, tying together the mechanics from this chapter with real, tradable consequences on the NSE.
